title: Enzyme Kinetics: Km, Vmax and Where the Lines Meet
summary: Read the Michaelis–Menten curve and the Lineweaver–Burk plot, tell competitive, noncompetitive and uncompetitive inhibition apart, and see why labs measure initial rates and dilute samples with very high activity.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 21 Hit 1 (inhibition patterns), Hit 5 (Lineweaver–Burk intercepts and slope), Hit 6 (Km; rate ∝ enzyme at saturation; initial velocity), Trap 3 (endpoint assays falsely low with very high activity) and the Figure 21 anchor. Checked against Robinson 2015 and Ramsay & Tipton 2017; intercepts and the parallel uncompetitive line follow from the rearranged equations. Pending: Km = (k−1 + k2)/k1 expression.

objectives: Define Vmax and Km from the Michaelis–Menten curve and explain why assays use excess substrate and initial rates.
Read the Lineweaver–Burk plot (intercepts and slope) and identify competitive, noncompetitive and uncompetitive inhibition.
Explain why an endpoint assay can under-report very high enzyme activity and how dilution fixes it.

scenes.title: A “normal” amylase in severe pancreatitis
scenes.altText: A patient with classic severe pancreatitis pain: lipase 1,200 U/L. The fixed-time (endpoint) amylase result comes back “normal”. A puzzled token asks how an enzyme result can be falsely low. The answer: enzyme kinetics.

cues.text: A patient has severe upper abdominal pain. The lipase is very high.
But the amylase, measured with a fixed-time endpoint method, comes back normal.
Can an enormous amount of enzyme ever read as normal? To answer that, you need to know how enzymes behave.

scenes.title: Normal: the Michaelis–Menten curve
scenes.altText: Axes: reaction rate (v) against substrate concentration [S]. Points trace a hyperbola that rises steeply, then flattens toward a ceiling, Vmax. A dashed line marks Vmax/2; dropping to the [S] axis marks Km — the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity. A low Km means the enzyme is half-saturated at low substrate (high affinity). At saturating substrate, rate is proportional to the amount of enzyme — which is why enzyme assays supply excess substrate and measure the initial rate.

cues.text: Add more substrate and an enzyme works faster — at first. Then the curve flattens, because every enzyme molecule is busy. That ceiling is V-max.
Halfway up, at V-max over two, drop down to the substrate axis. That substrate concentration is K-m, the Michaelis constant.
A low K-m means the enzyme reaches half speed with only a little substrate. We read that as high affinity.
When substrate is in excess, rate depends only on how much enzyme there is: double the enzyme, double the rate. That is why enzyme assays add plenty of substrate and measure the initial rate.

scenes.title: What changes: inhibitors on the double-reciprocal plot
scenes.altText: Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot: 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line. Y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax. Then three inhibitor lines are added in turn. Competitive (binds the active site; overcome by more substrate): Km rises, Vmax unchanged — the line pivots and meets the original on the y-axis. Noncompetitive (binds elsewhere, removes active enzyme): Vmax falls, Km unchanged — lines meet on the x-axis. Uncompetitive (binds only the enzyme–substrate complex): both fall — a parallel line.

cues.text: Flip both axes — one over rate against one over substrate — and the curve becomes a straight line. It crosses the y-axis at one over V-max, and the x-axis at minus one over K-m.
A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and sits in the active site. Enough substrate outcompetes it, so V-max is unchanged, but K-m rises. The new line meets the old one on the y-axis.
A noncompetitive inhibitor binds somewhere else and simply takes enzyme out of action. V-max falls; K-m stays the same. The lines meet on the x-axis.
An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only to enzyme that already holds substrate. Both V-max and K-m fall by the same factor, so the line shifts up but stays parallel.

scenes.title: In the lab: measure the straight part
scenes.altText: A progress curve: product formed against time, straight at first, then bending flat. Causes listed: substrate depletion, product inhibition, approaching equilibrium, instability. A kinetic assay reads the slope (ΔA/min) in the straight, initial part. Second curve: a sample with enormous activity uses up substrate within seconds; a fixed-time endpoint reading taken later sees a flattened curve and under-reports. Remedy: dilute and re-run; kinetic methods flag the non-linearity.

cues.text: Follow an enzyme reaction over time. At first, product builds in a straight line. Then the curve bends and flattens.
Why? The substrate runs out, products start inhibiting the enzyme, the reaction nears equilibrium, or a component breaks down.
So labs measure the initial rate — the slope of the straight part. Kinetic methods read the change in absorbance per minute, and can detect when the line stops being straight.

Now a sample with enormous activity. It burns through the substrate within seconds. A single endpoint reading taken later sees a flat curve and under-reports. The fix: dilute the sample and run it again.

props.label: Kinetic: ΔA/min in the straight part
High activity (ringed): flat early → endpoint falsely low

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Any inhibitor lowers Vmax” is crossed out → “Competitive: Vmax unchanged, Km up — more substrate overcomes it.” Trap card: “Uncompetitive is the same as noncompetitive” is crossed out → “Uncompetitive lowers Km and Vmax (parallel lines); noncompetitive lowers only Vmax.” Trap card: “A normal endpoint result rules out high activity” is crossed out → “Substrate depletion can make it falsely low — dilute.”

cues.text: Trap one: not every inhibitor lowers V-max. A competitive inhibitor raises K-m, and enough substrate restores full speed.
Trap two: uncompetitive is not noncompetitive. Uncompetitive lowers both K-m and V-max — parallel lines. Noncompetitive lowers only V-max — lines meet on the x-axis.
Trap three: a normal endpoint result doesn’t rule out very high activity. If the substrate ran out early, the result is falsely low — dilute and repeat.

props.title: ✗ “Every inhibitor lowers Vmax.”
lines: ✓ Competitive: Km ↑, Vmax unchanged — excess substrate overcomes it

props.title: ✗ “Uncompetitive = noncompetitive.”
lines: ✓ Uncompetitive: Km ↓ and Vmax ↓ (parallel) · noncompetitive: Vmax ↓ only

props.title: ✗ “A normal endpoint result rules out high activity.”
lines: ✓ Substrate depletion can make it falsely low — dilute

scenes.title: Where the lines meet
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Competitors fight at the door (y-axis); noncompetitors sabotage the factory (x-axis); uncompetitors trap the busy workers (parallel).” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: competitive lines meet on the y-axis, noncompetitive on the x-axis, and uncompetitive lines never meet — they run parallel.

Where it breaks: many real inhibitors are mixed, and some authors use “noncompetitive” loosely for mixed inhibition. The double-reciprocal plot is good for showing patterns but inaccurate for estimating K-m and V-max; curve fitting is preferred.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Many inhibitors are mixed · “noncompetitive” is used loosely
Double-reciprocal plots show patterns but estimate Km/Vmax poorly

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Km = [S] at Vmax/2; measure the initial rate with excess substrate”, “Competitive Km↑ · noncompetitive Vmax↓ · uncompetitive both↓”.

cues.text: Km is the substrate level at half Vmax; enzyme assays measure the initial rate with excess substrate, and inhibitors are told apart by what they do to Km and Vmax.

props.label: Km = [S] at Vmax/2 · measure the initial rate
Competitive Km↑ · noncompetitive Vmax↓ · uncompetitive both↓

explanation.what: Plain language: an enzyme speeds up as you give it more substrate until every enzyme molecule is busy; inhibitors slow it down in different ways. Scientific terms: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity; the Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v vs 1/[S]) is linear with y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km and slope Km/Vmax.
explanation.why: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site, so excess substrate displaces them (Vmax unchanged, apparent Km increased). Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and remove active enzyme (Vmax decreased, Km unchanged). Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Vmax and apparent Km by the same factor (parallel lines).
explanation.measure: At saturating substrate, initial rate is proportional to enzyme concentration, so clinical assays supply excess substrate and measure the initial (linear) rate. Progress curves flatten because of substrate depletion, product inhibition, approach to equilibrium or instability; with very high activity, an endpoint reading can be falsely low — dilute and re-run.
explanation.differs: Competitive (y-axis intersection) vs noncompetitive (x-axis intersection) vs uncompetitive (parallel); kinetic (rate) vs fixed-time endpoint methods.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identifying inhibition type from Km/Vmax changes or plot shape, reading Km and Vmax from intercepts, Km = [S] at Vmax/2, and the “falsely normal endpoint” trap.

mnemonic.text: Where do the lines meet? Competitive → y-axis; noncompetitive → x-axis; uncompetitive → never (parallel).
mnemonic.explanation: Competitive keeps Vmax (same 1/Vmax intercept); noncompetitive keeps Km (same −1/Km intercept); uncompetitive keeps the slope Km/Vmax.
mnemonic.limitation: Many inhibitors are mixed; “noncompetitive” is used loosely by some authors; double-reciprocal plots are inaccurate for estimating parameters — nonlinear fitting is preferred.

analogyLimitations: Plots are idealised with Km = 1 and Vmax = 1, not real data.
Mixed and partial inhibition are not shown.
takeaway: Km is the substrate level at half Vmax; enzyme assays measure the initial rate with excess substrate, and inhibitors are told apart by what they do to Km and Vmax.

questions.stem: In the presence of an inhibitor, Vmax is unchanged and the apparent Km increases. Which type of inhibition is this?

options.rationale: Correct. Excess substrate outcompetes the inhibitor at the active site, so Vmax is reached but more substrate is needed for half-maximal rate.
Incorrect. Noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax and leaves Km unchanged.
Incorrect. Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Vmax and apparent Km.
Incorrect. Irreversible inhibition removes active enzyme, lowering Vmax.

questions.stem: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the line crosses the y-axis at 0.5 and the x-axis at −0.25 (consistent units). What are Vmax and Km?

options.rationale: Correct. Y-intercept = 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 2; x-intercept = −1/Km, so Km = 4.
Incorrect. The intercepts are reciprocals, not the values themselves.
Incorrect. The intercepts have been swapped.
Incorrect. Km is the negative reciprocal of the x-intercept, which gives 4.

questions.stem: A fixed-time (endpoint) enzyme result is unexpectedly normal in a patient whose other findings suggest extremely high activity. What is the best next step?

options.text: Dilute the sample and re-run, or use a kinetic method
options.rationale: Correct. Very high activity can exhaust the substrate before the reading, flattening the curve; dilution restores linearity.
Incorrect. Substrate depletion can produce a falsely low endpoint result.
Incorrect. The same substrate depletion would recur.
Incorrect. A longer time makes depletion worse.
